chief_complaint: non-healing deep foot ulcer probing to bone
hpi_details: A 77-year-old male presents to the clinic with non-healing deep foot ulcer probing to bone. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the sore is just a stubborn blister from stiff new walking shoes that is taking a long time to close because of his diabetic poor circulation.
concerns: He is terrified that the deep infection won't heal and that doctors will have to amputate his foot, just like his older brother experienced.
expectations: He hopes to receive specialized medicated dressings and antibiotics so he can treat the wound at home without needing a hospital stay.
pmh: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus diagnosed 15 years ago, complicated by peripheral neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease; hypertension.
medications: Metformin 1000mg BID, Insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime, Lisinopril 10mg daily.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Diabetic Osteomyelitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Plan for Diabetic Osteomyelitis: Bone biopsy and culture, prolonged IV antibiotics, surgical debridement, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: non-healing deep foot ulcer probing to bone

Key HPI features: A 77-year-old male presents to the clinic with non-healing deep foot ulcer probing to bone. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.6C, HR 88, BP 138/82. Deep plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head with visible bone at the base, positive probe-to-bone test, surrounding erythema and mild cellulitis. Diminished sensation to 10g monofilament testing, diminished pedal pulses. ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP elevated. Plain foot X-ray shows cortical erosion and periosteal reaction of the first metatarsal; MRI confirms bone marrow edema consistent with osteomyelitis.
Relevant background/PMH: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus diagnosed 15 years ago, complicated by peripheral neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease; hypertension.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Diabetic Osteomyelitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cellulitis alone (no bone involvement) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Systemic signs of infection (fever) — suggests spreading infection.
management_principles: Plan for Diabetic Osteomyelitis: Bone biopsy and culture, prolonged IV antibiotics, surgical debridement
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: non-healing deep foot ulcer probing to bone

A 77-year-old male with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes complicated by peripheral neuropathy presents to the clinic with a non-healing deep foot ulcer probing to bone. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.6C, HR 88, BP 138/82. Deep plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head with visible bone at the base, positive probe-to-bone test, surrounding erythema and mild cellulitis. Diminished sensation to 10g monofilament testing, diminished pedal pulses. ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP elevated. Plain foot X-ray shows cortical erosion and periosteal reaction of the first metatarsal; MRI confirms bone marrow edema consistent with osteomyelitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Diabetic (foot ulcer-associated) Osteomyelitis of the first metatarsal, supported by a positive probe-to-bone test, elevated inflammatory markers, and MRI findings, in a patient with longstanding diabetic neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease.
reference_soap.plan: Assess severity, perfusion, and need for urgent drainage; obtain plain films and MRI when needed. Obtain deep tissue or bone culture when feasible before antibiotics if this will not delay necessary treatment. Use culture-directed antibiotics by oral or IV route according to severity and bioavailability, and involve wound-care, vascular, infectious-disease, and surgical teams for selective debridement or revascularization.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Diabetic Osteomyelitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Diabetic Osteomyelitis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Bone biopsy and culture, prolonged IV antibiotics, surgical debridement

teaching.one_liner: A chronic bone infection arising from a non-healing diabetic foot ulcer that has progressed deep enough to probe to bone.
red_flags: Systemic signs of infection (fever) — suggests spreading infection

must_ask.say: How long has this ulcer been there without healing?
Has a doctor ever probed this wound down to the bone?
How well controlled is your diabetes?
Can you feel your foot normally, or has it gone numb?
Any fever or feeling generally unwell?

history.answer: I noticed an open sore on the bottom of my right foot that just will not heal, and it seems to be getting deeper.
I think I stepped on a small pebble or had a tight shoe rubbing against it a few weeks ago, but I did not feel it right away.
The sore appeared about four weeks ago, and over the past week it has gotten deeper and wider.
It is on the ball of my right foot right beneath the big toe, about the size of a coin, and looks like a deep crater.
I wash it daily with clean tap water, and I do not recall stepping on any rusty nails or having dirt trapped inside.
It does not bleed much, just a little oozing fluid and some yellowish discharge on my socks.
My feet have felt numb and tingly for years, but I can still wiggle and bend my toes normally.
No, I have not had any burns from hot water, fire, chemicals, or heating pads.
Surprisingly, it barely hurts because my feet are numb, though I feel a dull ache if I stand on it.
It has been open for about a month, and I have only been putting over-the-counter antibiotic ointment and dry bandages on it.
There is some mild redness and warmth spreading around the edges of the sore over the last few days.
There is a faint unpleasant odor and a bit of yellowish pus, and I have felt slightly warm and fatigued lately.
I walk around the house every day and do not stay in bed, but my feet lose feeling when I walk.
Yes, my calves often ache and feel tight when I walk a block or two, and it goes away when I rest.
I received a tetanus booster about five years ago after a minor scrape in the garden.
I do not take any blood thinners, steroids, or medications that weaken my immune system.
No, absolutely nothing like that; this was purely an accidental sore on my foot.
When I looked closely with a mirror, the bottom of the sore looked hard and whitish, like bone is exposed.
My home blood sugars usually run between 140 and 180, and my last A1c was around 8.2 percent three months ago.
I have been feeling unusually tired and run-down over the past few days, though I have not had shaking chills.
I have had type 2 diabetes for 15 years with nerve damage and poor circulation in my legs, along with high blood pressure.
I had my appendix removed when I was in my twenties, but no other surgeries or hospital stays.
I take metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, 20 units of glargine insulin at bedtime, and lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink an occasional glass of beer with dinner, maybe once or twice a month.
I am a retired postal worker and live at home with my wife.
My father had type 2 diabetes and died of a heart attack in his seventies, but my mother lived into her eighties.
I figured it was just a nasty blister from my new walking shoes that is having trouble closing up because of my poor circulation.
I'm terrified that this sore is going to get worse and that I'll end up losing my foot, just like what happened to my older brother.
I was hoping you could give me some special wound dressings and antibiotics so I can treat this at home instead of being admitted to the hospital.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Elderly male resting comfortably, appears mildly fatigued, in no acute distress.

A 2 cm deep circular ulcer over the plantar aspect of the right first metatarsal head with visible bone at the base, positive probe-to-bone contact, and 1 to 2 cm of surrounding erythema and warmth without fluctuance or crepitus.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are markedly diminished bilaterally; capillary refill is delayed at 4 seconds in the right toes.
Diminished sensation to 10g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament testing and decreased vibration sense in a stocking distribution on both feet.
Active flexion and extension of all toes and ankles are intact bilaterally with 5/5 motor strength.
Mild non-pitting edema around the right forefoot; no pitting edema of the ankles or lower legs.
Calves are soft, non-tender, and symmetric without swelling, cords, or calf pain on dorsiflexion.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezing, rales, or rhonchi.
